Cloud sessions in Claude Code

How Sigma runs in a Claude Code web session: a container with a lifetime, a fresh clone, no local files, and what survives when it ends.

On this page
  • What a cloud session is, for Sigma
  • What is different from a local session
  • The token and the 403
  • --land unattended
  • Checkpoint and resume
  • Known flakes
  • Starting a cloud batch
  • When a session hits the container lifetime

Most people only need

  • A cloud session is temporary: anything not pushed to GitHub is lost when it ends.
  • One named issue goes to a merged pull request with /sigma-goal N --land.
  • Read The token and the 403 before the first run.
  • GitHub access is REST only there: gh issue and gh pr list and view do not work.
  • A full cloud batch with checkpoint and resume has not been measured in a real container.

A cloud session is a temporary computer that clones your repository, does one job and is deleted. Sigma can take one named issue to a merged pull request inside it with /sigma-goal N --land. Because the machine disappears, anything that matters is pushed to GitHub early, and a new session picks up from there. Several things work differently from your laptop, and one thing is not yet proven: nobody has measured a full cloud batch with checkpoint and resume or known-flake handling in a real container.

What a cloud session is, for Sigma

FactConsequence
A container with a lifetimeIt is deleted after the session. Anything not on GitHub is lost.
A fresh clone every timeNo local trust, no cached state, no earlier action log. The operator approves the verify command once per environment, as a hash in the environment's variables. It is a hash, not a secret, and only the operator sets it, never an agent.
No local filesGit-ignored plans, research and acceptance records are gone with the container. For a GitHub-backed goal, a durable copy of the reviewed plan is left as a comment on the issue after a confirmed merge.
No setup wizardThe session start skips the wizard question when it detects a cloud session.

What is different from a local session

AreaIn the cloud
GitHub accessREST first. A proxy sits in front of GitHub and GraphQL is not available, so the gh issue and gh pr list and view commands do not work. Sigma reads and writes with REST instead.
Projects boardSkipped, with one notice.
Auto-mergeNot armed with gh pr merge --auto. Sigma waits for pending checks (work.merge_pending_wait_s, default 450 seconds) and parks if the base does not require them. Arming through the Claude Code cloud route is unconfirmed.
Review approvalrequire_review: approval is met by the post-PR review's sigma:approve comment, because the review decision cannot be read.
Line commentsAny comment on the pull request parks it for a person: thread resolution cannot be read.
Background helpersNo watcher runs. With the team ledger on, entries are published at the claim, the lease renewal and the outcome, and once as the process exits normally. A container torn down by a termination signal runs no exit hook.
Resource guardLimits are derived from the container, which is small. One measured run in a 2 GiB Linux container: an unguarded arm lost 2 of 4 verifies to the kernel and the guarded arm lost none. The ratios are policy defaults, not calibrated.

The token and the 403

A cloud token can read what it needs on the repository and still be refused when reading branch protection: the classic protection read answered 403 with "Resource not accessible by integration" while the rulesets read answered (seen in two cloud sessions, and in a real container on 13 November). That 403 belongs to the credential, not the branch.

Sigma treats the base as unprotected only when all three hold: the protection read was a permission 403, the rulesets read returned a list with nothing counted, and the branch's own protected flag is exactly false. Anything else (a 404, a server error, a rate limit, a missing or true flag) fails closed: the goal is parked with a plain note saying why the loop did not merge. The fallback path itself was not reached in a live run, because that repository has no unprotected base.

A repository whose ruleset reports every pull request as blocked can opt in to merging through the account's ruleset bypass with work.merge_bypass: "ruleset". It merges only when four conditions read over REST all hold, and parks and names the failing one otherwise.

--land unattended

Start one container per issue and run /sigma-goal N --land. It refuses up front unless work.enabled is on and work.auto_merge is protected or always. It takes the goal only when the loop's own picker would, runs the phases with no gate pauses, and ends in exactly one of merged, parked or failed. In the cloud it parks on: a check still pending after the wait that the base does not require, any pull request line comment, or a protection read it cannot determine. A pull request left awaiting merge is not finished by any machine once the container is gone, so its body must say Closes #N for GitHub to close the issue on merge. See Running unattended.

Checkpoint and resume

The goal branch is pushed after each implement commit and before every full verify, so a container that dies during the long verify keeps the code. The push is a plain fast-forward and is never forced. A refused push (a path or content scan caught something) pushes nothing and says how to fix it; a push that merely fails prints a warning and the run continues, because the checkpoint is a safety copy, not a gate.

When a new session starts the same goalWhat happens
The branch holds commits the base lacks and its pull request did not mergeResumed: the base is merged into it, the plan must match the issue's durable copy, and the run goes forward from the first open phase. Plan-review, review and verify evidence are not carried over, so each runs again.
Merge conflict, changed or missing plan copy, merged pull request, unreadable state, or a leftover branch it cannot account forThe old branch is left exactly as it is. The work goes on <branch>-2 (then -3, the first name free on the remote) and the issue gets a note naming both. A person removes the old branch.
The remote branch moved under the checkpoint pushA warning names the fix (merge the remote branch in, then checkpoint again) and the run continues.

The setting work.checkpoint_prefix (default empty: the goal branch itself) sends checkpoints to, say, wip/<N>, so a workflow that runs on pushes to goal branches does not run on unverified code. A new container has no earlier action log, so a resume there re-enters at the implement phase.

Known flakes

verify.known_flakes lets a project lead approve a time-limited exception for named flaky tests. A person adds each entry with the approval record; Sigma never adds one. When a full verify fails and every failing test matches an unexpired entry covering the goal's base, each is re-run alone on the same head. If all pass, the evidence is passed-with-known-flakes, not passed; the pull request body says so, and the post-PR review must end with KNOWN-FLAKES: accept or reject.

It acceptsIt fails closed (verify stays red) on
Only pytest failures that match an unexpired entry for that base, and pass when re-run aloneA malformed setting (the whole list is ignored), an unmatched failure, an expired entry or one not covering the base, a solo re-run that fails or times out, a changed tree, and output that cannot be trusted to list every failure

It never skips, quarantines or loosens a test. The integration branch is never covered by a wildcard. Another test runner reads as "no failing id" and stays red. Full rules: Configuration.

Starting a cloud batch

  1. Approve the verify command once in the environment's variables (the doctor prints the value to paste).
  2. Set work.enabled and work.auto_merge as above, and check the account can read branch protection or accept a parked ending.
  3. Answer the four readiness questions: is the dependency bot paused if CI is paused, does the environment start every service the suite needs, do the tests avoid ambient tokens and local databases, and does the base pass its verify command.
  4. Keep the launch prompt to /sigma-goal N --land plus facts about the environment. Gate edits, actions on other pull requests and extra rules in the prompt caused refusals and parks in the first real wave.
  5. For a batch, use /sigma-orchestrate --where cloud --dry-run first. See Running many goals.

When a session hits the container lifetime

  • If the dead run left its claim (the issue still carries sdlc:in-progress), a new /sigma-goal N --land reports "not taken": --land never reclaims a claim. A person releases it first with the loop's release command (documented in the land reference); its audit comment names the checkpoint branch. If the pull request already merged, close the issue instead and do not re-run.
  • Then start /sigma-goal N --land in a new session. It resumes from the checkpoint branch or moves to -2, as above.
  • An unscoped /sigma-loop pick reclaims a claim whose lease (12 hours by default) has run out, but only where the team ledger is on and holds the dead run's claim.
  • Code not yet pushed, and a plan that was git-ignored with no issue copy, are lost.
What is not measured

A real end-to-end cloud batch has not been run: checkpoint and resume were tested against a local bare remote and known-flake handling against real pytest re-runs, but neither has run in a real cloud container, and the docs state that Sigma is not claimed to support the whole loop in a cloud session. Measured live in a real container: the 403 on the protection read, and the setup wizard being silent. Not measured: the 403 fallback through to a merged pull request, a proxy's reply to every comment and merge call, and the cost of a cloud goal. This page rests on the documentation, not on a run, wherever it says otherwise.

Technical detail

A cloud session is detected from the environment (CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE true or 1), with SIGMA_GH_GRAPHQL=off|on as the operator override that takes precedence; no network probe runs by default. Sources: cloud sessions, configuration, platform support, orchestrate.
